final.title: Why stopping rules fall short in small-business workflows
final.body:
Stopping rules sound neat until you meet the real workflow. In a small business, the problem is usually not the first rule. It is the exception: the invoice that is over the usual amount, the customer record that is incomplete, the lead that looks promising but needs a human eye. A simple if-then rule can stop work, but it can also stop the wrong work or let the wrong thing through. That is why a bounded automation decision should start with the exception path, not the happy path.

The practical question is simple: in your repeated workflow, what judgment calls do you keep making by hand that a fixed rule would miss? If the answer is “almost none,” AI probably is not worth the trouble. If the answer is “quite a few,” map the exceptions on one page. Mark which ones are safe to route to a person, which ones can be checked automatically, and which ones must stay human-only.

That last part matters most where money is involved. Bareni’s boundary is clear: human approval stays in place for payments and other high-risk decisions. The system can flag, sort, and prepare work; it should not quietly decide on the risky bit. Less glamorous, more useful. Usually the right choice.

If your workflow already lives in digital documents and SaaS tools, and it repeats often enough to have a measurable outcome, that one-page exception map is the next step. It gives you a grounded decision: keep it manual, hire for it, or automate only the parts that do not need judgment.
